summary: AstroScan is an interactive decision-support web application that compares planned lunar rover traverses with candidate Earth analog test routes. Instead of matching broad regions by visual similarity alone, AstroScan evaluates path-specific similarities up to 75 km across a unified 90 m metric grid. Users select two lunar coordinates and a mission objective—Rover Navigation, Camera/Lighting, or Mineral Mapping—and our routing solver computes a feasible lunar path while searching volcanic and arid Earth terrains (including Harrat Khaybar, Payún Matrú, Pinacate, and custom coordinates) for the closest statistical match. By combining NASA SLDEM2015, Copernicus GLO-30, SPICE solar geometry, and M3/EMIT hyperspectral reflectance data via 1D Wasserstein distance scoring, AstroScan quantifies slope, roughness, 30-day lighting windows, and mineral absorption bands. Crucially, it flags data coverage gaps and where Earth analogies break down, giving mission teams traceable, exportable evidence before committing to costly field trials.
details:
AstroScan helps lunar mission researchers find places on Earth where they can test rover navigation, cameras, and mineral mapping techniques. A user picks two points on the Moon and selects a test objective. AstroScan calculates a traverse, searches for Earth routes with similar terrain, and ranks the candidates based on what matters for that test. Researchers can compare elevation profiles, slopes, roughness, and, where comparable data is available, modeled shadows and mineral spectra.

The creative part is that AstroScan compares specific routes, so researchers can see where the similarities occur. For example, selecting a slope range in the terrain chart highlights the corresponding stretches on both maps. The same lunar traverse can also produce different rankings depending on the test objective. A camera team can prioritize lighting, while a rover team can give more weight to slope and roughness. The app shows which evidence contributed to each ranking and how the order changes when the weights shift.

We built the web interface with React, TypeScript, Leaflet, and Vite, and the analysis backend with Python and FastAPI. The backend uses A* to plan routes on an elevation grid and Wasserstein distance to compare terrain distributions. NASA and JAXA lunar elevation data and Copernicus Earth elevation data support the terrain analysis. NASA SPICE supports lighting calculations, while Chandrayaan‑1 M³ and NASA EMIT provide reflectance data for mineral comparisons.

We designed AstroScan to help teams decide where to investigate and what to test before committing time and resources to fieldwork. We considered terrain resolution, incomplete data, and how research priorities affect rankings. The 90 m grid captures broad terrain features, while rocks, traction, wheel slip, weather, and site safety still require field checks.
